newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria bags rival CA after bitter battle. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria bags rival CA after bitter battle. [CORRECTED 23:30 GMT]

text.p: Austria wrapped up Europe's longest privatisation in the early hours of Sunday by selling key bank Creditanstalt to former arch-rival Bank Austria, ushering in a shakeup of the nation's bloated banking sector.

After an 11-hour crisis meeting of coalition leaders the feuding partners hammered out a deal that let both sides save face and which they said was in the best interest of both the Austrian taxpayer and the country's financial system.

"The sale was successful, especially for the interests of the Austrian taxpayer and for shareholders of Creditanstalt. We managed to get the best possible price," a visibly relieved Finance Minister Viktor Klima told a news conference.

The sale of Creditanstalt, erstwhile banker to the Habsburg family of Austro-Hungarian emperors, split the coalition of dominant Social Democrats and conservative People's Party and pushed the government to the verge of collapse.
"What we have achieved is a significant step towards ensuring Austrian interests and the withdrawal of politics from economic matters," Social Democrat Klima said.

The conservatives lost their main battle -- to save blue-blooded Creditanstalt from being sold to Bank Austria, which is controlled by the Social-Democratic led City of Vienna -- but scored on a range of side issues that are likely to make the deal more expensive for Bank Austria than projected.

Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa told Reuters that the integration of Creditanstalt would cost the bank a hefty sum but that the synergies from the merger would nevertheless ensure improved earnings for 1997.
"The charges against earnings will be substantial -- and still our earnings will be better in 1997," he said.
Creditanstalt, established in 1855 to finance the development of the Austrian Empire's railway network, will retain its independence for the next five years.
Over the next seven (corrects from five) years, Bank Austria will gradually be taken out of public control. Full privatisation of Austria's top bank was the main stumbling block in the negotiations.
Another conservative demand was to ensure that Creditanstalt's small shareholders receive a competitive price.

Klima said Bank Austria would offer small shareholders an extra 2 schillings ($0.18) per ordinary share to buy the 30 percent of voting shares not yet owned by the state -- a paltry premium of 0.3 percent over their market price.

According to the coalition agreement, the state's 19 percent stake in Bank Austria will be floated immediately, while the 45 percent stake held by the City of Vienna's Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation is to be cut to below 20 percent within seven years.
AVZ guarantees Bank Austria's liabilities, ensuring it a AAA rating, but the conservatives want AVZ's financial responsibility removed fully, which would likely cost Bank Austria its top-rating.

A group of international financial and industrial interests led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali made little effort to hide its dismay at having been outbid by Bank Austria by almost three billion schillings.
"We regret the decision...We submitted the most attractive offer for the long-term good of Austria's economy," EA-Generali chief Dietrich Karner said in a tightly-worded statement.
The link-up of Austria's two top banks will create a financial powerhouse with some 1,300 billion schillings in total assets, holding wide-ranging stakes in many of the country's blue-chip companies.
Together, the two banks wield almost total control over Austria's overcrowded retail banking sector, raising the likelihood of a large number of branch closures and job cuts. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
